prompt: In a pull arrangement, what starts a Puppet run on one of the shop's servers?
hint: Look at which side opens the conversation in the figure.

choices.text: The Puppet server, as soon as a manifest changes
choices.why: The server waits to be asked; it compiles a catalogue when an agent connects.

choices.text: An SSH connection from Ana's laptop
choices.why: That is push, the way lesson 18 runs Ansible.

choices.text: The agent on that server, on its timer
choices.why: Yes. The agent asks the server what the machine should be, every `runinterval` seconds.

choices.text: A person typing `puppet apply` on it
choices.why: That is the serverless mode this lesson uses in the lab, not the pull arrangement.

prompt: `puppet config print` showed `runinterval = 1800`. How many minutes apart are an agent's runs?
hint: The value is in seconds.

prompt: At 10:12 somebody edits nginx's file by hand on a server whose Puppet agent runs with the default settings. What happens to the edit?
hint: The agent compares on every run.

choices.text: It stays until somebody runs Puppet by hand
choices.why: That is what happens under push; an agent does not wait for anybody.

choices.text: The next agent run writes the described file back, within half an hour
choices.why: Right. The next run finds a difference and writes the file as described.

choices.text: The agent refuses the write as it is typed
choices.why: The agent is not watching the file; it compares only when it runs.

choices.text: The server copies the edit into the manifest
choices.why: Nothing ever writes back into the description; the description wins.

prompt: During a night outage the on-call engineer fixes it by editing a file on a server that runs a Puppet agent. The outage ends. What does the lesson say about the morning after?
hint: The agent cannot tell a fix from a mistake.

choices.text: The fix is safe, because the agent leaves files a person edited
choices.why: It has no idea who edited a file; it only sees a difference.

choices.text: The agent reverts it, and the outage returns
choices.why: Yes, unless the fix went into the manifest. The description is the one place a change lasts.

choices.text: The agent stops running until somebody re-enables it
choices.why: A hand edit does not stop an agent; it is exactly what the agent corrects.

choices.text: The server records the edit as the new desired state
choices.why: Nothing flows from the machine back into the description.

prompt: Which of these are costs the lesson gives for the pull arrangement? Choose all that apply.
hint: Software on every machine has a price.

choices.text: An agent to install, upgrade and keep running on each machine
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A server that every machine has to reach
choices.why: Yes, and it needs backing up.

choices.text: Certificates to issue and revoke
choices.why: Yes; each agent proves who it is with one.

choices.text: The control machine reaching every target at the moment of the run
choices.why: That is the cost of push, where one machine connects out.

choices.text: A hand edit that lasts until somebody runs the tool again
choices.why: That is push too; an agent corrects it on its next run.

prompt: Why does the lesson place Salt between push and pull?
hint: Who opens the connection, and who sends the commands?

choices.text: It needs no agent, like Ansible, but polls like Puppet
choices.why: Salt does have an agent, the minion.

choices.text: Minions connect out; the master sends commands down at once
choices.why: Right: the machine opens the connection, as with pull, and the master acts immediately, as with push.

choices.text: It alternates, pulling on even hours and pushing on odd ones
choices.why: There is no such schedule; the difference is who opens the connection and who starts the run.

choices.text: It runs over SSH only
choices.why: `salt-ssh` exists, but a minion keeps its own connection to the master.

prompt: `puppet apply` printed `Compiled catalog for laptop`. What is the catalogue?
hint: With an agent, the server sends it down.

choices.text: A cache of the packages Puppet has downloaded
choices.why: Puppet keeps no such list; the catalogue is about resources.

choices.text: The manifest worked out for one machine
choices.why: Yes: every resource, variables filled in, relationships resolved.

choices.text: The list of machines the Puppet server knows about
choices.why: It is for one machine, named after `for`.

choices.text: The certificate issued to the machine called `laptop`
choices.why: The certname names the machine; the catalogue is what it should contain.

prompt: The second `puppet apply site.pp` printed only the compile and apply lines, with no `Notice` for any resource. Why?
hint: Compare with the first run.

choices.text: It ran in `--noop` mode by default the second time
choices.why: `--noop` prints what it would change; nothing needed changing.

choices.text: Every resource already matched the manifest, so there was nothing to do
choices.why: Right. That is idempotency: a run where everything is as described does nothing.

choices.text: Puppet applies each manifest only once per machine
choices.why: It applies it every time; an agent does so every thirty minutes.

choices.text: The catalogue was reused from the first run without being checked
choices.why: Each resource was checked; checking found nothing to do.

prompt: `puppet apply --___ server.pp` compares the manifest with the machine and reports what it would change, without changing anything.
hint: Four letters: no operation.

prompt: After the first apply, a hand edit, and the third apply, `cat` printed `reloads.log`. How many lines did it hold?
hint: The `exec` runs only when `shop.conf` changes.

prompt: Run as Ana without `--noop`, `server.pp` failed to install nginx. Why did Puppet not try the file and the service at all?
hint: Read the two `Skipping` lines.

choices.text: Puppet stops a manifest at its first error
choices.why: It carries on with resources that do not depend on the failure; these two did.

choices.text: Ana is not root, so everything under `/etc` was skipped in advance
choices.why: The skip message names a failed dependency, not a path or a user.

choices.text: They depend on the package, which failed
choices.why: Right. `require` and `notify` put them after the package in the graph, and a resource whose dependency failed is skipped.

choices.text: A failed resource makes Puppet switch to `--noop` for the rest
choices.why: There is no such switch; they were skipped, not simulated.

prompt: `puppet resource package nginx` printed `provider => 'apt'`. What does provider mean here?
hint: Not the Terraform meaning.

choices.text: The Terraform provider that installed nginx
choices.why: Terraform is not involved, and in Terraform the word names a program for a cloud's API.

choices.text: The mirror the package is downloaded from
choices.why: Where `apt` downloads from is apt's own configuration.

choices.text: The backend that turns the type into apt commands
choices.why: Yes. The same type gets a different provider on another system.

choices.text: The module on the Puppet Forge that defines packages
choices.why: `package` is a built-in type, not a Forge module.

prompt: In Salt, what are grains?
hint: `grains.item os` answered `Ubuntu`.

choices.text: Data a master hands to chosen minions, secrets among it
choices.why: That is pillar.

choices.text: The states inside an `.sls` file
choices.why: States are the descriptions; grains are facts.

choices.text: Facts a minion gathers about its machine
choices.why: Yes, like the operating system that `web.sls` wrote into the page.

choices.text: The minions a top file targets
choices.why: The top file targets minions by id or pattern, such as `'*'`.

prompt: Match each Salt word to what it is.
hint: One of the right-hand items belongs to no word.

pairs.right: Which states apply to which minions

prompt: Salt's dry run, the counterpart of Puppet's `--noop`, is `salt-call --local state.apply test=___`.
hint: A boolean, written the way Python writes it.

prompt: On the second `state.apply`, `reload-web` reported `Clean`. Why did the command not run?
hint: Look at its requisite.

choices.text: `cmd.run` runs only on a minion's first apply
choices.why: It ran again after the hand edit, on a later apply.

choices.text: Salt remembered the result of the first run and reused it
choices.why: Salt checked the page; the command is skipped because the page did not change.

choices.text: `test=True` was still in effect from the dry run
choices.why: Each `salt-call` is separate; the second apply had no `test=True`.

choices.text: `onchanges` saw no change
choices.why: Right: it runs the command only when `index.html` changed, and nothing did.

prompt: What does `file_client: local` change in Ana's minion configuration?
hint: It is the masterless switch.

choices.text: States are read from the machine's own disk
choices.why: Yes, from `file_roots`, instead of from a master.

choices.text: Salt writes its logs and cache under Ana's directory
choices.why: That is `root_dir`.

choices.text: The minion runs without root
choices.why: That is `user: ana`.

choices.text: The minion looks for a master on the local network instead of the internet
choices.why: With `file_client: local` it does not look for a master at all.

prompt: A mistyped Jinja condition in `web.sls` leaves one block out, and the YAML that comes out is still valid. What does the lesson suggest for seeing what Salt will do?
hint: The file Salt reads is not the file you wrote.

choices.text: Run a YAML linter over `web.sls`
choices.why: The file you wrote is not YAML yet, and what comes out is valid YAML anyway.

choices.text: Read the rendered states with `state.show_sls`
choices.why: Yes: it shows what Salt received after Jinja ran, missing block included.

choices.text: Check the summary of a `test=True` run for a failure
choices.why: Nothing fails: a block that is absent is simply not run.

choices.text: Compare the grains before and after with `grains.item`
choices.why: The grains did not change; the template did.

prompt: Why does the Chef section show a recipe with no output beside it?
hint: Look at its first capture.

choices.text: Chef prints nothing when a run succeeds
choices.why: It does print; the lesson simply had no Chef to run.

choices.text: Recipes cannot run without a Chef Infra Server
choices.why: Local mode runs them without a server.

choices.text: Chef is not installed in the lab, and output nobody ran would be invented
choices.why: Right. The last block of the captures shows that none of Chef's commands exist there.

choices.text: Its output is the same as Puppet's, so it would repeat
choices.why: The output is different; it was left out because nothing was run.

prompt: A recipe has a line of plain Ruby, between two resources, that reads the file the first resource creates. On a fresh machine, what does that line find?
hint: Chef reads a run in two phases.

choices.text: The file, since Chef applies everything in the order written
choices.why: Resources converge in order, but plain Ruby ran earlier, while the resources were being collected.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right: it ran in the first phase, before any resource was applied.

choices.text: An error, because Chef refuses Ruby outside a resource
choices.why: A recipe is Ruby; any Ruby is allowed, which is the source of the surprise.

choices.text: The file's content from the template
choices.why: The template has not been rendered when that line runs.

prompt: Put the steps that take a changed cookbook to a machine running `chef-client` against a server in order.
hint: The workstation first, the convergence last.
items: Upload the cookbook to the Chef Infra Server with `knife`
`chef-client` fetches the run-list and the cookbooks it needs
The Ruby of every recipe is evaluated and the resources collected
Each resource is converged, in the order it was written
trap: Evaluating and converging are not the same step: the Ruby runs before any resource is applied.

prompt: A job advert asks for experience with Cinc. What is it?
hint: The recipes are the same.

choices.text: Chef's command-line tool for uploading cookbooks
choices.why: That is `knife`.

choices.text: The template format Chef renders
choices.why: That is ERB.

choices.text: A community build of Chef's open-source code under another name
choices.why: Yes, used where Chef's own binaries and their licence terms do not suit.

choices.text: Chef's server
choices.why: That is the Chef Infra Server.

prompt: Match each tool to what makes something run only when another thing changed.
hint: The last row of the table.

prompt: In which of the four tools is the order the resources are written in only a fallback?
hint: A graph comes first.

choices.text: Ansible
choices.why: Tasks run as written.

choices.text: Chef
choices.why: Resources converge as written.

choices.text: Salt
choices.why: File order, which a requisite can override.

choices.text: Puppet
choices.why: Yes: relationships decide, and the manifest order only where there are none.

prompt: A shop deploys by building a new image and replacing every web server; none lives more than a week. Which way of configuring them does the lesson favour?
hint: Short-lived machines have little time to drift.

choices.text: A Puppet agent on each, correcting drift every thirty minutes
choices.why: An agent earns its place on long-lived machines; here there is almost nothing to correct.

choices.text: Bake it into the image
choices.why: Right. Configuration moves into the image the machine is built from, which is lesson 20.

choices.text: A Salt master pushing `state.apply` to every minion each hour
choices.why: That keeps long-lived machines right; these are replaced before they drift.

choices.text: Chef in local mode on every boot
choices.why: It works, but it repeats at every boot what could be done once, in the image.

prompt: Which of these do Ansible, Puppet, Chef and Salt all share? Choose all that apply.
hint: The model under the syntax.

choices.text: Resources with a desired state
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: An agent installed on every machine
choices.why: Ansible has none; it connects over SSH.

choices.text: A run that acts only where something differs
choices.why: Yes; every second run in this lesson changed nothing.

choices.text: Descriptions written in YAML
choices.why: Puppet has its own language and Chef is Ruby.

choices.text: A way to say one resource depends on another
choices.why: Yes: `require`, a requisite, or the order of tasks and resources.

prompt: Match each tool to its way of showing what it would change without changing anything.
hint: One of them is lesson 18's.

prompt: Ana moves the `file` resource of `server.pp` into another manifest and drops its `require`. On a fresh server, what can now go wrong?
hint: Without a relationship, what decides the order?

choices.text: Nothing: Puppet sorts resources by type, packages first
choices.why: Puppet has no ordering by type; relationships decide, and without one the manifest order does.

choices.text: Puppet refuses to compile a file under `/etc` with no `require`
choices.why: A resource with no relationship compiles; that is why the risk is silent.

choices.text: Nothing orders the configuration after the package any more
choices.why: Right. The file can be written before nginx is installed, into a directory the package has not created yet.

choices.text: The service is restarted on every run
choices.why: Restarts come from `notify`, which was kept; the lost relationship is about order.

prompt: A company keeps 400 long-lived servers, and an auditor asks for proof each month that their configuration stayed as described. Which arrangement does the lesson's comparison point to?
hint: Who checks between the times somebody remembers?

choices.text: Ansible run by hand whenever a change is made
choices.why: Between runs nothing compares, so a hand edit can last for months unseen.

choices.text: New images for every change, with Packer
choices.why: That fits machines that are replaced; these are kept for years.

choices.text: An agent on each, correcting and reporting on every run
choices.why: Yes: long-lived machines under audit are where an agent pays for itself.

choices.text: Terraform, since it compares the description with what exists
choices.why: Terraform sees the cloud's resources, not files inside the machines.
